title: Uber broke the monolith. Then the pieces broke them.
subtitle: Two thousand microservices, fifty-service debugging, and the one rule that fixed it
hook: “Can't live with them, can't live without them.”
_vo: 20 beats. Rahil S, eleven_v3. Tags on 11 of 20 lines so the register CHANGES across the arc — confiding open, flat evidence, held turn, lifted payoff, quieter limitation. Contractions throughout; a synthetic mouth reads 'it isn't' as human and 'it is not' as legal.

vo.text: [whispers] One bug… fifty services. Twelve teams. [serious] That's what it took to find where it started.
Uber didn't have a scaling problem… [curious] They had the problem they created by SOLVING their scaling problem.
Chapter one. The escape.
Twenty thirteen. Two monoliths ran all of Uber. [serious] One bad regression could take the whole company down.
Deploys were painful. Rollbacks, constant. Every team's fate tied to every other team's code.
[excited] So they broke it apart. Independent deploys. Isolated failures. Teams that could finally move alone.
And it worked. [curious] That's the part everyone forgets… For years, it genuinely worked.
Chapter two. The cost.
By twenty twenty… twenty-two hundred critical microservices. Calls running many layers deep.
[serious] Finding one root cause meant fifty services, across twelve teams. The half-life of a service? Eighteen months.
And the worst of them only LOOKED independent. Deploy them together… or don't deploy at all.
[serious] Uber has a name for that. A networked monolith. All of the cost of distribution… none of the freedom.
So the instinct is to go back. [deadpan] Uber's own answer is blunt. There is no turning back.
Chapter three. Domains.
[curious] They stopped counting services… and started drawing domains. Twenty-two hundred services became seventy.
Five layers. One rule. A layer may only depend on the layers beneath it.
Every domain gets one door. And you extend it without touching it. Plugins for logic. Protobuf for data.
[excited] One team went from three DAYS to three hours. Onboarding down by up to half. Support costs down an order of magnitude.
[resigned] It isn't free. Half the domains are still unbuilt… and this is org design wearing an architecture diagram.
Microservices were never the mistake. [serious] Having no rule about who may depend on whom… THAT was the mistake.
